questions.question_text:
$F(x)=x^{4}+3x$.
For which function $f(x)$ is $F(x)$ a primitive?

options.why: Differentiated $x^{4}$ correctly but left the term $3x$ unchanged instead of differentiating it to $3$.
Treated $3x$ as a constant and differentiated it to $0$.
Found a primitive of $F(x)$ instead of differentiating $F(x)$.

questions.question_text: Which function has $F(x)=2x^{3}-5x^{2}$ as a primitive?

options.why: Reduced each power by $1$ but forgot to multiply by the original powers.
Multiplied each term by its power but did not reduce the powers by $1$.
Found a primitive of $F(x)$ instead of differentiating $F(x)$.

questions.question_text: Which of these functions is a primitive of $f(x)=10x^{9}$?

options.why: Kept the coefficient $10$ as well as raising the power, so differentiating gives $100x^{9}$.
Differentiated $f(x)$ instead of reversing the differentiation.
Left the power at $9$ instead of raising it by one to $10$.

questions.question_text:
One primitive of $f(x)=14x$ is $F(x)=7x^{2}$.
Which expression is the general primitive of $f(x)$?

options.why: Omitted the constant of integration, so this names only one primitive rather than the whole family.
Attached the constant to $x$; differentiating this gives $14x+C$, not $14x$.
Added $C$ to $f(x)$ instead of to the primitive $F(x)$.

questions.question_text:
$P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are both primitives of the same function $f(x)$.
Which statement must be true?

options.why: Assumes primitives are unique, but two primitives may differ by any constant.
Treats the difference as a varying function of $x$ rather than a fixed constant.

options.text: $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ differ by a multiple of $x$.
options.why: A difference of $kx$ would differentiate to $k$, so $P'(x)$ and $Q'(x)$ could not both equal $f(x)$.

questions.solution_text:
$P'(x)=f(x)$ and $Q'(x)=f(x)$
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(P(x)-Q(x))=f(x)-f(x)$
$=0$
A function with derivative zero everywhere is constant, so $P(x)-Q(x)$ is a constant.

questions.question_text:
The graph of $y=h(x)$ has a horizontal tangent at every point.
Which statement describes $h(x)$?

options.text: $h(x)$ is a linear function with non-zero gradient.
options.why: A non-zero gradient gives a non-zero derivative, so the tangent would never be horizontal.
$y=x$ has gradient $1$ everywhere, so its tangent is never horizontal.

options.text: $h(x)$ is any function with one stationary point.
options.why: One stationary point gives a horizontal tangent at a single $x$-value, not at every point.

questions.solution_text:
A horizontal tangent everywhere means $h'(x)=0$ for all $x$.
Only a constant function has a derivative of zero everywhere.
So $h(x)$ is a constant function.

questions.question_text:
The rule that a primitive of $x^{n}$ is $\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$ works for every real $n$ except $n=-1$.
Why is $n=-1$ excluded?

options.text: It would make the denominator $n+1$ equal to zero.
A negative index makes the function negative, and the rule needs positive values.
options.why: A negative index does not make the function negative, and the rule works for $n=-2$.
$x^{-2}$ is also undefined at $x=0$ yet the rule applies to it, so this is not the reason.

options.text: Raising the power by one gives $x^{0}=1$, which has no primitive.
options.why: $x^{0}=1$ does have a primitive, namely $x$; the failure is the zero denominator.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$ with $n=-1$
$=\dfrac{x^{0}}{0}$
Dividing by zero is undefined, so the rule cannot be used when $n=-1$.

questions.question_text:
$F(x)=x^{4}$ is a primitive of $4x^{3}$ and $G(x)=x^{9}$ is a primitive of $9x^{8}$.
Which function is a primitive of $9x^{8}+4x^{3}$?

options.why: Multiplied the two primitives together instead of adding them.
Kept the coefficients $9$ and $4$ as well as raising the powers, so differentiating gives $81x^{8}+16x^{3}$.
Averaged the two primitives; the sum rule adds them and does not halve the result.
